name: New York
note: In New York the funeral director drives registration. They collect the informant's particulars, get the medical certificate from the attending practitioner (or the coroner/ME), and file through the state Electronic Death Registration System within 72 hours, which unlocks the burial or removal permit. New York City is a separate registration area under its own Health Code. From registration, death records flow monthly to the state board of elections for cancelling voter registrations. Federal benefit agencies are reached through the federal layer.

steps.title: Informant supplies the personal particulars to the funeral director
steps.who: A competent person acquainted with the facts (usually next of kin).
steps.summary: The funeral director gets the decedent's identifying and demographic details from an informant and records the informant's name and address on the certificate.

steps.title: Funeral director presents the certificate for medical certification
steps.who: The funeral director, undertaker or person in charge of the body.
steps.summary: The funeral director presents the certificate promptly to the attending physician or nurse practitioner, or to the coroner, medical examiner or hospital official as applicable. Since the EDRS implementation date this is done through the system.

steps.title: Hospital gets the attending practitioner to certify promptly
steps.who: The person in charge of the hospital or a designee.
steps.trigger: A death in hospital (not a coroner/ME case).

deadline.text: in time to meet the 72-hour registration limit

steps.summary: For a hospital death the hospital must promptly give the certificate to the attending physician or nurse practitioner. That clinician must certify and return it in time for the 72-hour registration limit.

steps.title: Physician or nurse practitioner certifies the cause of death
steps.who: The physician or nurse practitioner last in attendance on the deceased.
steps.summary: The practitioner last in attendance makes, dates and signs the medical certificate. Symptom-only causes are not accepted, and opioid overdose deaths must be noted. Section 4141 sets no separate hour limit; the 72-hour registration limit controls.

steps.title: Deaths without medical attendance are reported to the coroner or medical examiner
steps.who: The funeral director, undertaker or any other person who learns of the death.
steps.summary: Anyone who learns of a death without medical attendance, including the funeral director, must report it to the coroner or medical examiner (in Erie County, the medical director).

steps.title: Coroner or medical examiner investigates and certifies
steps.who: The county coroner or medical examiner.
steps.summary: The coroner or medical examiner investigates at once and issues the certificate, stating the cause and whether the death appears accidental, suicidal or homicidal.

steps.title: Funeral director files the death certificate with the local registrar within 72 hours
steps.who: The funeral director, undertaker or person in charge of the body.
steps.trigger: Completion of the certificate; before disposition.

deadline.text: immediately and not later than seventy-two hours after death or the finding of the body

steps.summary: The death must be registered with the registrar of the district where it occurred within 72 hours of death or of finding the body, and before the remains are disposed of. Since the EDRS implementation date, deaths are registered through the state's Electronic Death Registration System; the rollout could be phased.

steps.title: Registrar issues the burial or removal permit
steps.who: The local registrar of the district where the death occurred.
steps.trigger: Filing of a properly completed death certificate.
steps.summary: Registration gates disposition: the registrar issues the burial or removal permit only once the certificate is properly completed. Cemeteries and crematories may not accept a body without a permit, and must return endorsed permits to the registrar within seven days.

steps.title: New York City registers deaths under its own system
steps.who: Funeral directors and certifiers in the five boroughs, filing with the NYC Department of Health and Mental Hygiene.
steps.trigger: A death in New York City.
steps.summary: Article 41 mostly does not apply to New York City, which is a separate registration area under the NYC Health Code. The city's own deadline, electronic system and copy rules were not verified. The city health department sends the state board of elections its own monthly death records.

steps.title: Certified copies only to relatives, those with a legal right, agencies, or by court order
steps.who: The commissioner of health or an authorized person (registrar).
steps.summary: Certified copies go to the spouse, domestic partner, children, siblings or parents, or the agent controlling disposition. They also go to anyone showing a documented medical need or a legal right or claim, to government agencies for official purposes, to approved research, or by court order. Death records are excluded from freedom-of-information disclosure.

steps.title: Monthly death records to the state board of elections, then to county boards, which cancel
steps.who: The state commissioner of health and the NYC Department of Health, to the state board of elections, which sends them on to the local boards.
steps.trigger: Issue of death certificates for persons of voting age.
steps.summary: At least monthly, the state health department and the NYC health department send the state board of elections, county by county, the records of every person of voting age for whom a death certificate was issued. The state board passes them to the county boards, and death is a ground for cancelling registration.

registrationDeadlineDays.note: 72 hours after death or finding of the body, and before disposition (outside NYC; the NYC Health Code was not verified).

informantDuty.note: The funeral director or person in charge of the body files; the informant only supplies the personal particulars.

medicalExaminerScrutiny.note: No independent review of ordinary certificates. Coroner or medical examiner involvement is triggered only by deaths without medical attendance and other medicolegal cases.

electronicRegistration.note: PHL 4148 requires deaths in the state to be registered through the Electronic Death Registration System (it allowed a phased rollout); NYC runs its own system (not verified).

certificateAccess.note: Close relatives, people with a documented legal right or claim, agencies, approved research, or a court order.

gaps: assembly.state.ny.us (www and apex) and nyassembly.gov were refused at the egress proxy (CONNECT 403). nysenate.gov answers curl with a Cloudflare challenge but could be read through the WebFetch tool, so all quotes come from nysenate.gov pages read that way.

NYC Health Code article 205 (NYC registration deadline, eVital system, NYC certificate access) could not be read: nyc.gov, www1.nyc.gov and rules.cityofnewyork.us were blocked. The NYC step is unverified.
No pronouncement provision was found (PHL 4140-A does not exist; RN pronouncement rules under Education Law or 10 NYCRR not searched). The pronounce stage is empty.
How a local registrar sends records on to the state vital records office, and the state's 405(r) / EDR contract with SSA, were not sourced in New York law.
No New York provision was found for death notification to the DMV, Department of Taxation and Finance, or Medicaid. health.ny.gov and dos.ny.gov were blocked.
PHL 4174's open-access rule for older death records (genealogy, if any) was not found in the text read.
